title: Asynchronous Emergence of Water Scarcity Risks Amid Shifting Hydrological Regimes in High Mountain Asia
content:
Abstract

High Mountain Asia functions as a critical hydrological hub, supporting water security and the livelihoods of billions downstream. However, reliable assessments of future water availability remain limited because the contributions and future changes of individual runoff components have not been explicitly quantified. Here, we use a distributed hydrological model constrained by multisource observations to analyze runoff components and dynamics across 12 major basins. Our partitioning analysis shows that groundwater, which acts as a key subsurface storage and routing pathway for infiltrated precipitation and meltwater, accounts for 15.07% of total runoff, exceeding the combined contribution of glacier melt (5.60%) and snowmelt (4.46%). Anthropogenic aerosols exhibit a strong negative influence on runoff changes, largely offsetting greenhouse-gas-driven wetting, particularly in the arid northwest. By combining these hydroclimatic changes with demographic projections, we identify a marked mid-century turning point around 2060, when the population exposed to water scarcity reaches 1.04–1.51 billion; by 2100, the exposed population diverges to 0.72–1.94 billion across shared socioeconomic pathways. These risks are uneven across basins, with earlier emergence in inland basins and a later, larger peak in the Indus and Brahmaputra & Ganges basins, underscoring the need for basin-specific transboundary actions that prioritize groundwater protection and demand management before mid-century.
